record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: Find (in explicit form) a variety of ℓ-groups that has no finite basis of laws but every proper subvariety has a finite basis of laws.

evidence.quote: 1.8. Find (in explicit form) a variety of ℓ-groups that has no finite basis of laws but every proper subvariety has a finite basis of laws.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Recall that a lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is an algebra (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over the lattice operations on both sides (i.e. a(b∧c)d = abd ∧ acd and a(b∨c)d = abd ∨ acd for all a,b,c,d ∈ G). A variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups defined by a set of equational laws (equivalently, closed under taking subalgebras, homomorphic images, and direct products). A variety V is said to have a finite basis of laws if it can be axiomatized (relative to the variety of all ℓ-groups) by finitely many equations. A subvariety of V is a subclass that is itself a variety; it is proper if it is not equal to V.

Exhibit, in explicit form, a variety V of ℓ-groups such that:
(i) V has no finite basis of laws, and
(ii) every proper subvariety of V has a finite basis of laws.

(Such a variety is called a limit variety of ℓ-groups.)
artifact.category_tag: lattice-ordered groups, varieties and equational bases
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface an explicit construction of a limit variety of ℓ-groups (a nonfinitely based variety all of whose proper subvarieties are finitely based). The general concept of "limit variety" is well-studied in universal algebra (e.g., for semirings and semigroups), but no resolution specifically for ℓ-groups was located, so the status here is recorded as unknown.
